case_studies.title: CAVA: Canonical Action Verification and Attestation for Runtime Governance of Agentic AI Systems
case_studies.abstract: Agentic AI systems increasingly act through heterogeneous runtimes: local coding hooks, SDK tools, browser automation, managed-agent traces, API gateways, and workflow engines. A single operational act such as publishing code, changing identity state, moving money, or exporting data may therefore be represented by many incompatible runtime records. This makes a basic governance question difficult to answer: what action was actually approved, what evidence binds the approval to execution, and can an independent verifier reproduce the same action identity later? case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of verifying actions in AI systems that run on different platforms, by building a system called CAVA that checks and confirms what actions were taken. CAVA ensures that actions are correctly approved and executed, and provides evidence for independent verification. The result is improved governance and trust in AI systems.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI systems or infrastructure that uses AI, here is what to do: review your current governance processes, assess how CAVA can be applied to your systems, and consider implementing it to improve trust and verification of AI actions.
case_studies.relevance_tag: AI governance, runtime verification, agentic systems
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a novel framework (CAVA) for runtime governance of agentic AI systems, specifically addressing the challenge of verifying actions across heterogeneous runtimes. This is IT-relevant as it affects how IT engineers ensure the security and integrity of AI systems. The value within 90 days is high as IT engineers can apply this framework to improve runtime governance, automate verification processes, and identify potential security risks.

case_studies.title: Copy-on-Write Scoring: Application-Specific Agent Evaluations
case_studies.abstract: Trustworthy deployment of LLM-based agents in software systems requires evaluating how they perform on application-specific workflows, with enough granularity to localize where they succeed and fail. Yet existing agent evaluation mechanisms are limited: benchmarks have low construct validity for application-specific workflows and environments, and replica evaluation environments are expensive and prone to drift. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluating the performance of Large Language Model (LLM) agents in specific software systems, by building a framework called Copy-on-Write Scoring, which resulted in more accurate and granular evaluation of agent operations. The framework uses a PostgreSQL-level Copy-on-Write mechanism to isolate and evaluate agent operations. This research helps in the trustworthy deployment of LLM-based agents in software systems.

case_studies.title: Rubrics on Trial: Evolving Rubrics from a Single Query via Synthetic Pairwise Evidence
case_studies.abstract: Rubrics provide structured, fine-grained signals for training and evaluating large language models (LLMs). Yet reliable query-specific rubrics are difficult to construct. Existing approaches often derive supervision from human-written rubrics, preference data, or sampled responses. Direct query-to-rubric generation avoids these resources, but provides no explicit check that a plausible rubric is useful. Such a rubric may fail to distinguish answer quality, reward an optional style, or penalize a valid alternative strategy. We introduce Rubrics on Trial, a query-only framework that evolves a ru
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of creating reliable query-specific rubrics for training large language models, by introducing a framework that evolves rubrics from a single query via synthetic pairwise evidence, resulting in more effective and useful rubrics. The researchers built a query-only framework called Rubrics on Trial. This framework helps to improve the quality of large language models.

case_studies.title: Partition, Prompt, Aggregate: Statistical Self-Consistency in Language Models
case_studies.abstract: In-context learning is commonly interpreted as a form of conditional inference, in which the prompt specifies a context and the model's output is treated as an estimate of the corresponding conditional distribution. If this interpretation holds, then LLM estimates should satisfy basic probabilistic identities. In particular, the law of total probability asserts that prior-weighted conditional distributions aggregate into population-level marginals over any valid partition of the population. In this work, we investigate to what extent LLM estimates adhere to this self-consistency principle. We
case_studies.summary: This research investigates if language models can produce statistically self-consistent estimates, which is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work. The authors built a framework to test the self-consistency principle in language models. The result shows how well language models adhere to basic probabilistic identities.

case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper discusses a novel aspect of LLMs, in-context learning, and statistical self-consistency. It may not have an immediate practical impact but has some IT relevance due to its focus on LLMs. However, its immediate value remains unclear.

case_studies.title: When Words Are Safe But Actions Kill: Probing Physical Danger Beyond Text Safety in Hidden-State Risk Space
case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as high-level planners for embodied agents, where linguistically benign instructions can become unsafe once grounded in the physical world. We study whether this physically grounded danger is the same safety problem as ordinary text-level content danger. Through hidden-state direction analysis and random-split null tests, we show that content danger (CD) and physical danger (PD) form separable signals in LLM representations across Qwen2.5-3B/7B/14B/32B, Phi-3.5 and SmolLM2. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of identifying physical dangers that may not be apparent in text-based instructions, by building a model called PRISM that separates content danger and physical danger signals in large language models, resulting in a more accurate assessment of potential risks. It shows that physically grounded danger is a distinct safety problem from ordinary text-level content danger. This study may have implications for IT infrastructure work related to AI and machine learning applications.

case_studies.title: Scaling Behavior Foundation Model for Humanoid Robots
